# Setup Microsoft Teams for the Agent SDK

The user brings an Azure Bot: its Microsoft App ID, a client secret,
and the App Tenant ID. Cursor does not create the bot. Never print the
client secret, and never pass it on argv.

Teams has no Socket Mode. Azure posts each activity to a public HTTPS
messaging endpoint, so local dev needs a tunnel. `agent-sdk dev` opens
a cloudflared quick tunnel and prints that endpoint. `cloudflared` must
be on PATH. `--tunnel devtunnel` uses a Microsoft dev tunnel instead,
which keeps one URL across restarts.

Guide: `docs/guides/teams.md`.

## 1. Azure Bot (human)

`agent-sdk channels teams setup` prints these steps. Stop and ask the user to:

1. Create an **Azure Bot** in the Azure portal. Type of App: **Single
   Tenant**. Creation type: **Create new Microsoft App ID**.
2. On **Configuration**, copy the **Microsoft App ID** and the **App
   Tenant ID**.
3. **Manage Password** → **New client secret**. Copy the secret value.
4. **Channels** → **Microsoft Teams** → **Apply**.

## 2. Credentials

```bash
printf %s "$CLIENT_SECRET" | agent-sdk channels teams init --dir . \
  --app-id <microsoft-app-id> --tenant-id <app-tenant-id>
```

On a terminal, drop the pipe, and the user types the secret at the hidden
prompt. `init` checks that both ids are GUIDs, writes
`bot/channels/teams.ts` when it is missing, and writes
`TEAMS_APP_ID`, `TEAMS_APP_PASSWORD`, and `TEAMS_TENANT_ID` to
`.env.local` (mode 600, gitignored).

For one Azure Bot per agent in a multi-agent serve, pass
`--prefix JENNY`. `init` then writes `envPrefix: "JENNY"` into the new
channel file and the `JENNY_TEAMS_*` names. The prefix must start with a
letter. When `bot/channels/teams.ts` exists, `init` keeps it and writes
the names it reads; a `--prefix` that disagrees stops with an error.
Rerun `init` to rotate the secret. `--dry-run` reads no secret and
writes nothing.

## 3. App package (human uploads)

```bash
agent-sdk channels teams package --dir .
```

It writes `<slug>-teams-app.zip` (`manifest.json`, a color icon, and
an outline icon) and adds `*-teams-app.zip` to `.gitignore`.
`--out <file>` writes it elsewhere. The manifest names the bot by its
app id and lists the scopes the channel answers in. With
`engagement.channelPosts`, it also asks for `ChannelMessage.Read.Group`
consent. `--name` sets the app name. `--icon` takes a 192 by 192 PNG.
`--app-version` sets the version. The default grows with the time, so
a new zip updates the app. After a custom `--app-version` such as
`2.0.0`, the default is lower and Teams refuses the update, so keep
passing a higher version.

Ask the user to upload the zip in Teams: **Apps** → **Manage your
apps** → **Upload an app**. A Teams admin can publish it to the
organization from the Teams admin center instead. To update the app,
build a new zip and upload it the same way.

## 4. Serve

```bash
agent-sdk dev .
```

`dev` prints `Teams messaging endpoint:` and a URL such as
`https://<random>.trycloudflare.com/jenny/v1/channels/teams`. Ask the
user to set it on the Azure Bot: **Configuration** → **Messaging
endpoint** → **Apply**. The cloudflared URL changes each time `dev`
starts, so set it again after a restart.

To set it once, use a dev tunnel. The user must run `devtunnel user
login` first.

```bash
agent-sdk dev . --tunnel devtunnel
```

The first start creates the tunnel and saves `TEAMS_DEVTUNNEL_ID` in
`.env.local`. Later starts print the same URL. Microsoft deletes a dev
tunnel after 30 days without use, and the next start creates it again
under the same id. The tunnel owns port 3978, so run the agent on
another `--port`. The tunnel stops when it publishes any other port;
remove that port with `devtunnel port delete <id> -p <port>`.

Next to a plain `agent-sdk serve`, `agent-sdk channels teams forward --dir .`
opens the same tunnel and takes the same `--tunnel` flags. The tunnel
forwards only `POST` to the Teams messaging paths. Every other path on
it is a 404, so sessions, tools, MCP, and evals stay local.

## 5. Doctor

```bash
agent-sdk channels teams doctor --dir . --endpoint <printed URL>
```

`doctor` reads the env names the loaded channel declares. Green is `env`, `token`, `bot-tenant`, `bot-endpoint`,
`teams-channel`, and `endpoint`.

- `token`: Entra issued a Bot Framework token, so the app id, secret,
  and tenant match.
- `bot-tenant`: the Azure Bot is Single Tenant, in the tenant the
  channel's tenant id variable holds. Any other bot type fails.
- `endpoint`: the URL's path names this channel, and an unsigned `POST`
  got `401`: `invalid_token` from the channel, or `Unauthorized` from
  Cursor-managed hosting. `503 teams_not_configured` means the server
  lacks the secrets. `404` or a path for another channel means a wrong
  URL.
- A channel that sets `credentials` in code has no env names to read:
  doctor prints `env: set in code` and skips `env`, `token`, and the Azure
  checks; `package` and `init` stop with an error.
- `bot-tenant`, `bot-endpoint`, and `teams-channel` need a logged-in
  Azure CLI (`az login`). Without it they are skipped (`--`), not
  passed. When no Azure Bot in the subscription has the app id, they
  fail.

## 6. Smoke test (human)

1. **Channels** → **Microsoft Teams** → **Open in Teams** starts a 1:1
   chat.
2. For channels and group chats, add the uploaded app to the team or
   chat.
3. `@mention` the bot or send it a message.
